name: John Lennon
role: English musician, Beatles co-founder and peace and left-wing activist (1940-1980)
summary: Lennon was a working-class-identified songwriter whose politics moved from the anti-war pacifism of 'Give Peace a Chance' and 'Imagine' to a brief embrace of New Left revolutionary and socialist rhetoric in 1971-72. In his last interviews (1980) he said he was 'not anything', rejected following leaders and ideologies, and kept his stance against violence. He campaigned for peace, women's liberation and radical causes, and opposed the Vietnam War.

universal-healthcare.rationale: In 1980 he said he was an 'instinctive socialist' who thought people should get their false teeth and health looked after.

unions-good.rationale: He opposes the anti-union Industrial Relations Bill and identifies with the labor movement in his later account.

worker-ownership.rationale: 1971: said the workers 'can start to take over' and that he would like to see how workers' control worked in Yugoslavia; no detailed programme.

strong-leader.rationale: He rejects political leaders as substitute fathers expected to perform miracles.

empower-police-military.rationale: 1971: said a working-class upbringing teaches you to hate and fear the police and despise the army, though that wears off with age; songs 'Attica State' decry police brutality. No statement on funding.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

nation-first.rationale: In 1980 he described the message of 'Imagine' as picturing a world without countries; this runs against putting national interest first.

open-borders.rationale: His song 'Imagine' asks for a world without countries, which he restated in 1980; in 1973 he announced the conceptual state of Nutopia with 'no boundaries, no passports'.

revolution-justified.rationale: 1970-71: said a revolution 'has to happen' eventually and that 'you can't take power without a struggle'; but his 1980 view is that he wants to see the plan and will not join violence. Mixed record.

political-violence-never.rationale: His 1980 interview rejects violence for political change and reaffirms peaceful protest ('unless it is with flowers'); the recent clear position wins over his 1971-72 remarks accepting struggle and siding with the IRA over the British army, which keep it from the strongest value.

war-builds-character.rationale: Inferred: from his statements that the Vietnam War was a waste and should end, and his 'Give Peace a Chance' campaigns.

direct-action.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

means-match-ends.rationale: Peace-themed protest (bed-ins, 'Give Peace a Chance') and the 1980 line that he would stand on the barricades only 'with flowers' suggest methods matching aims, but he did not state the principle.

distribute-by-need.rationale: 1971: cited Marx's 'To each according to his need' and said 'I think that would work well here'. He called himself 'not anything' in 1980.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: He refused to perform to racially segregated audiences and the Jacksonville concert proceeded with mixed seating.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: 1971: said men are taught male superiority from childhood and that a revolution must liberate women; 1980: said the women's movement had barely begun to change society and men had not contemplated equality.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Said that the people in power and the class system were unchanged and in 1980 said politicians are 'daddies' people elect and then punish; he also said society is run by 'insane people'. Did not specifically allege corruption.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: In December 1980 he positively presents his interracial marriage as standing for love, peace and feminism.

vanguard-party.rationale: 1971: said revolutions came when intellectuals got through to workers who had not woken up, and that revolutionaries must approach the workers; did not mention a disciplined party.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: He criticizes the 1971 Industrial Relations Bill as an unenforceable attack workers would refuse to cooperate with.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: 1971: called the Oz obscenity prosecution 'disgusting fascism' and the censoring of his lyrics by EMI 'ridiculous and hypocritical'.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: No recorded position on aid between countries; his 1980 remark was about the Beatles donating money, which is something nearby.

leader-cult.rationale: 1971: said revolutions end up with personality cults and noted Khrushchev's view that making a religion of an individual was bad, though he wondered if it was necessary. 1980: 'Don't follow leaders'; the messenger is worshipped in place of the message.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: 1971: said workers are 'doped' by culture, 'dreaming someone else's dream' of cars and televisions, and that the owners control newspapers and distribution; 'Working Class Hero' says the same of pop stardom.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: 1971: said the aim is to break the dream workers are surrounded by, because they think they live in a free country and let the bosses run them.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: 1971: criticised workers who think 'cars and tellies are the answer'; but in 1980 said he had worked for money and wanted to be rich.

religion-illusion.rationale: In 1971 he endorsed Janov's line that religion is 'legalised madness' and said therapy dissolved his 'God shit'; in 1980 he said he was not anti-religion and was 'a most religious fellow'. He did not link religion's fading to material conditions.

participatory-democracy.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: 1971: said 'they own all the newspapers and they control all distribution and promotion' and that the capitalist press only quotes union mouthpieces.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: 1971: said he and Ono had a '50-50 relationship or there was no relationship'; 1980: described becoming a househusband and dropping his male-macho role.

religions-one-truth.rationale: 1980: said Christianity, Buddhism and others each carry a good piece of truth, that 'all the roads lead to Rome', and that people worship the messenger instead of the message.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: His 1970 song 'God' lists the Bible among things he does not believe in; in the 1970 interview he described the song as shedding myth.

notes:
Most recent clear position wins: in 1980 he distanced himself from the 1971 revolutionary stance (he said the 'Power to the People' period came partly from guilt), keeping only 'count me out' for violence. Red Mole and Playboy full texts were read; Rolling Stone 1970 book scan searched. Many stated causes (Attica, Sinclair, Ireland) have no matching statement beyond those answered. The Counterpunch original was blocked; a TRANSCEND reprint was used.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 9 answers taken from it, 8 agreed, 1 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass, existing audit read only for notes and sources. Full September and December 1980 interviews downloaded and searched alongside the estate’s compilation of earlier interviews and letters. Speaker attribution is essential: Ono’s answers, Ali’s and Blackburn’s arguments, and posthumous comments are not Lennon’s. No song lyrics quoted or used alone as policy evidence. His 1980 reaffirmation of pacifism and criticism of political father figures take precedence over the less settled 1971 revolutionary discussion. Nutopia is explicitly conceptual performance art, so its institutional details are low confidence and not turned into detailed constitutional or economic policy. All 490 statement texts and remaining nulls reviewed. Targeted searches for electoral rules, national identity, ecology, technology and international economic institutions yielded little specific evidence; modern AI documentary makers’ views are not his. No inference from marriage, party labels, drug use or wealth alone. Of the ten priority statements only discourage-race-mixing is answered directly; broad equal-rights, racial-franchise and constitutional claims stay null. Final specificity review leaves state-harmful null: an imaginary country without ordinary laws is not a sufficient statement that actual states are unnecessary and harmful. No effort was made to clear salience by expanding generic peace or equality rhetoric into constitutional, weapons or environmental positions.
